newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - March 7.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - March 7.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

A secret report by the National Crime Authority has found that Australian organised criminals are fast adopting the characteristics of big business. Focusing on the most powerful and entrenched of Australia's organised crime groups, the East Coast Milieu, the report warns that many of the Mr Bigs of the underworld are willing to take bigger risks for bigger profits. Page 1.

The Federal opposition was leaked a document yesterday outlining planned cuts to health of A$1.3 billion for the May budget. Addressed to Health Minister Michael Wooldridge, the Australian Federal Police have been called in to investigate the leak of the four-page document. Page 2.

Australia is to appear before the World Trade Organisation for the first time, after Canada challenged a ban on fresh North American Salmon imports. The challenge if successful would see Australia forced to end the ban on salmon imports. Page 3.

The risks of tax avoidance for businesses operating at airports after they are sold by the Federal Government has been the topic for urgent talks between State and Territory Governments with the Commonwealth. Due to uncertainty with tax collection, the Sates now want the Commonwealth to sell the land on which the airports operate - a solution which they say will not leave them reliant on the Commonwealth to return tax revenue collected. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Five army officers face disciplinary charges for their roles in a "chain of events" which culminated with the crash of two Black Hawk helicopters last year that killed 18 servicemen. A three-month investigation by a board of inquiry has exposed a chair o errors in the planning, command and execution of the ill-fated Black Hawk exercise near Townsville in June last year. Page 1.

The Victorian Government has failed to avert a 48-hour public transport strike, which threatens to plunge Melbourne into chaos as the city embarks on the Grand Prix weekend. A meeting of over 2000 workers voted to strike after failing to reach an agreement with the State Government on wages, working conditions and superannuation. Page 1.

The man who set alight a six-year-old school boy in a Cairns school last year was yesterday sentenced to life imprisonment. Paul Wade Streeton was found guilty of attempted unlawful killing, Justice Margaret White describing the crime as a cowardly attack by a bitter, obsessed man. Page 3.

Leaked documents for the upcoming budget outline cuts in childcare funding, higher drug prices and rises in medicare as key elements in Department of Finance plans to slash A$1.5 billion dollars from the health budget. The keys savings for the next four years are cuts in childcare funding of A$394 million and pharmaceutical costs of A$800 million. Page 6.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Thirty-six NSW teachers were removed from their classrooms yesterday and a former judge began reviewing investigations into another 106 teachers as the NSW Government tried to contain the political crisis over cover-ups of sexual abuse and harassment of students within the State's Education Department. The teachers involved have had their files passed to police to consider charges. Carr said he expected the inquiries of John Slattery, a former Supreme Court judge, would lead to the removal of more teacher. Page 1.

A secret Health Department document reveals the Federal Government plans massive cuts to prescription subsidies, child care and to charge more people a higher Medicare levy in a dramatic $1.36 billion slashing of the health budget. The document, prepared late last month and obtained by the Opposition, reveals that Cabinet's Expenditure Review Committee has demanded that Health Minister Michael Wooldridge cut spending by $152 million in 1997-98 and a further $324 million the next year. Page 1.

A long chain of events finalised with the 'inevitable outcome' of the Black Hawk helicopter crash on June 12 last year which killed 18 servicemen. A board of inquiry report into the disaster has found inadequate planning, lack of experience, and the helicpters flying off-track to a target all contributed to the crash. Page 1.

Sydney's largest teaching hospitals, the Prince of Wales Hospital Group and the South Eastern Sydney Area Health Service have been met with damming criticism in a review of hospital costs and efficiency. The report into the NSW's health system also concludes that by improving efficiency, the State's health service could save up to A$400 million annually. Page 3.
THE AGE

The army board of inquiry into the Black Hawk helicopter disaster found that a number of factors including: a lack of spare parts, corrosion problems and cracks in the airframe associated with external fuel tanks had virtually grounded the helicopter fleet in 1994 and 1995. The massive report makes it clear that the pilot of the lead helicopter, who died in the accident, was inexperienced and made the crucial final error which caused Australia's worst peacetime military disaster. Page 1.

Melbourne's biggest weekend of the year - the Australian Grand Prix and Moomba carnival - looks almost certain to be disrupted as public transport workers go on strike from midnight tonight, bringing trains, trams and buses to a halt for two days. Efforts to resolve the dispute failed yesterday when unions again rejected a State Government offer of a 6 per cent pay rise over 18 months. Page 1.

A study of birth defects has shown increasing numbers of women opting for abortions after discovering their unborn babies are malformed or defected. The report released by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare has shown a steep increase in the number of pregnancy terminations up to the 27th week by mothers with foetuses found to be suffering from serious problems such as spina bifida or Down's syndrome. Page 1.

A report by the Department of Employment, Education and Training has described Federal Government support for the unemployed as falling to an "unacceptably low level" in a damning internal report. It found subsidised job placements had not met Government targets and the placement of the unemployed into jobs was just half of that of October 1996. Page 1.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
